transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-02
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Nina Patel (LedgerByte Head of ML), Omar Al-Farouq (LedgerByte Infra), Hannah Kim (LedgerByte Product), Marcus Lee (SRE)

Auto-generated Summary (may be rough):
- Focus: Redwood Dedicated reserved capacity discussion for low-latency trading models.
- Key asks: hard isolation, predictable 95th percentile latency under burst, SOC2/ISO artifacts, price/term flexibility for reserved GPUs.

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the account executive on the Redwood side, and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Diego Alvarez: hi all, real quick agenda: 1) understand your current infra and workload; 2) sizing reserved capacity; 3) isolation & network requirements; 4) next steps to run a benchmark.
[00:18] Nina Patel: thanks, we'll do quick intros. I'm Nina, lead on model infra for trading signals. We do lots of short-lived inference around market opens, pretty spiky.
[00:28] Omar Al-Farouq: Omar, infra — we manage k8s clusters and some on-prem co-lo. Looking for options: hosted vs dedicated vs private vpn/vpc.
[00:36] Hannah Kim: Hannah, product — mostly responsible for SLA to our internal customers.
[00:40] Marcus Lee: Marcus, SRE, sorry I joined a few minutes late.
[00:45] Maya Chen: no worries. Nina, can you give a quick sense of traffic profile — qps and spike patterns?
[00:52] Nina Patel: baseline is about 30 qps across 5 models, but at market open it spikes to 500-700 qps over 2-3 minutes; per-call latency target is 50-100 ms 95th. We also have batch embedding jobs at night.
[01:12] Diego Alvarez: ok so bursts are intense but short. Two paths: Redwood Hosted + burst backfill or Redwood Dedicated with reserved pools plus burst capacity. Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs with isolation and guaranteed throughput.
[01:30] Nina Patel: what's the mechanism for burst? Like, if we reserve capacity, can we also buy temporary burst slices?
[01:38] Maya Chen: yes, we have configurable burst policies — you can allow bursts beyond reserved to use shared spare capacity on the fleet; there is a pricing delta. For high compliance customers we also offer dedicated-only burst pools (extra reserved) that you can spin up.
[01:50] Omar Al-Farouq: when you say isolation, does that include network-level VPC peering and tenant-level control plane separation? We can't have any co-tenancy on certain models.
[02:00] Diego Alvarez: there are several isolation layers. For Dedicated you get dedicated GPU pools and tenant isolation at the runtime layer; for Private (VPC) the control plane can be private and we provide VPC peering or private link and optional on-prem appliances. For your "no co-tenancy" models we can propose a private deployment or an isolated dedicated pool with restricted image set.
[02:22] Nina Patel: are there audited certificates? We need SOC2 and ISO docs to get procurement moving.
[02:27] Maya Chen: yes, we'll share SOC2 Type II, ISO/IEC certs, and our data handling and retention docs. I'll include those in the follow-up.
[02:34] Hannah Kim: curious how autoscaling works with reserved capacity. Does it queue or reject when you hit capacity?
[02:40] Diego Alvarez: by default Dedicated enforces soft limits: when reserved pool is saturated we can route to fallback model or queue with prioritization; you configure SLOs per route. There's also an option to scale up reserved capacity automatically if you have pre-approved burst credits.
[02:55] Nina Patel: queueing at market open for trading models is risky — we need sub-100ms tail; failing over to a fallback model with slightly degraded quality would be preferred to delayed responses.
[03:06] Diego Alvarez: good callout. We support automatic fallback to a lighter quantized variant or smaller model family with compatibility rules, so the application remains online with graceful degradation.
[03:18] Marcus Lee: question on KV cache / prefix caching — we depend on local KV for context window reuse. How does that work in Dedicated?
[03:26] Diego Alvarez: runtime supports KV cache pinning per instance; with Dedicated we can give you sticky routing so the same worker holds the cache for a session. Also support for multi-GPU KV sharding for large contexts.
[03:38] Omar Al-Farouq: what's the expected headroom we should reserve to meet 95th 100ms? Like if we need 500 qps bursts, do we reserve N GPUs or M?
[03:47] Diego Alvarez: rough back-of-envelope: depends on model and batch sizing. For large 7B-ish models at seq length 1024, an A100 equivalent can handle ~20-40 concurrent low-latency streams with batching; for your 700 qps spike with small tokens we'd likely recommend a pool of 16-24 GPUs with aggressive batching and fast KV caching. We'll run an exact benchmark.
[04:10] Nina Patel: can Redwood provide a benchmark fixture that mirrors our traffic? We can provide sample inputs and a time-of-day traffic trace.
[04:16] Maya Chen: absolutely — Diego will coordinate a perf run. Typically SEs ask for sample payloads, sequence length distribution, and tokenization characteristics. We'll run seq lengths 256/512/1024 and provide latency p50/p95/p99 and tokens/sec.
[04:30] Hannah Kim: cost is obviously big — what's the delta between hosted burst vs dedicated reserved?
[04:36] Maya Chen: reserved gives you predictability — lower per-token unit cost but requires commitment (monthly/annual). Hosted is pay as you go but higher unit cost, and bursts are subject to fleet availability. We can provide a cost model showing per-token cost vs reservation level.
[04:50] Omar Al-Farouq: any limits on custom kernels or our own model packaging? We often use custom ops.
[04:55] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated supports bringing validated model artifacts; custom kernels need validation but we do support a partner process. For strict private/on-prem we can accommodate fully custom runtimes.
[05:05] Nina Patel: we use an internal encryption key management requirement — keys must be customer-controlled in KMS/HSM. Is that supported?
[05:11] Maya Chen: yes, Private and Dedicated can integrate with customer KMS for key wrapping; for Hosted we have bring-your-own-key options in some regions. We'll include the KMS integration notes in the follow-up.
[05:20] Marcus Lee: SLO observability — we need per-route latency breakdowns, token-level cost, and traceability for audits.
[05:26] Diego Alvarez: Redwood Console exposes token-level cost, per-model latency heatmaps, request traces, and audit logs. For enterprise customers we can increase retention and provide exportable logs.
[05:40] Nina Patel: any hard guarantees on latency? We need to decide between guaranteed SLA and best-effort.
[05:46] Maya Chen: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets depending on the committed tier. We can discuss guaranteed 95th latency tiers in the contract; it requires capacity planning and potentially overprovisioning/priority queues.
[05:58] Hannah Kim: how much lead time for ramping reserved capacity? We might need to scale from dev to prod quickly over a month.
[06:05] Diego Alvarez: procurement and capacity carve-outs typically take 2-4 weeks for dedicated pools in the same region; private deployments or on-prem can take longer (4-8 weeks). We have expedited paths for urgent enterprise deals.
[06:16] Nina Patel: procurement question: can reserved capacity be seasonal? Our workloads are cyclical by quarter.
[06:22] Maya Chen: yes, we offer flexible commit profiles: monthly, quarterly, or annual, and you can tier capacity (base reserve + seasonal add-on). Pricing varies accordingly.
[06:32] Omar Al-Farouq: curious about failover — if a region loses capacity mid-trade, how do we failover without losing state?
[06:40] Diego Alvarez: our routing supports multi-region replication of model artifacts and async KV replication; for tight state requirements we recommend active-active with sticky routing and warm standby in a secondary region. We can also replicate the KV cache to durable storage between windows, but that adds latency cost.
[06:59] Nina Patel: will Redwood run a canary rollout and A/B traffic split for us? We need safe model rollouts.
[07:06] Diego Alvarez: yes, Redwood supports canaries and A/B routing with percentage-based rollout and automatic rollback if error/quality thresholds exceed.
[07:15] Marcus Lee: what's the typical tokenization overhead? We sometimes see tokenizer CPU bottlenecks.
[07:20] Diego Alvarez: we can offload tokenization to the runtime; for high throughput customers we recommend tokenization microservices colocated with workers or batch tokenization paths. We'll include recommendations in the benchmark report.
[07:33] Nina Patel: ok can we talk numbers? hypothetical: 16 GPUs reserved, 8 GPUs for burst — how would pricing look?
[07:40] Maya Chen: rough ballpark: reserved monthly fee X, burst usage billed at Y per GPU-hour; I'll send the matrix but to be transparent the reserved per-token cost can be 30-50% lower than pure hosted for sustained workloads.
[07:54] Hannah Kim: procurement will want a TCO spreadsheet.
[07:57] Maya Chen: we'll include that. Diego will produce a cost sensitivity table.
[08:03] Omar Al-Farouq: security: we need audit logs for who accessed model artifacts and request-level PII masking.
[08:10] Diego Alvarez: request-level PII redaction can be applied at the routing layer; audit logs are available and exportable to your SIEM. We'll include example retention options.
[08:21] Nina Patel: what's the process to get dedicated pool capacity pre-warmed before market open? We need no cold-starts.
[08:28] Diego Alvarez: we support warm pools and pre-warm scripts; you can schedule maintenance windows and keep a minimum warm replica count. That's commonly used for market-open bursts.
[08:38] Maya Chen: ok quick recap: Redwood will share SOC2/ISO docs, Dedicated pricing and reserve options, SE benchmark plan and a perf spreadsheet; customer will send sample payloads and traffic trace; schedule benchmark for next Tues.
[08:55] Nina Patel: that works. Marcus will own the VPC peering test.
[09:00] Marcus Lee: yep, I'll take that.
[09:03] Hannah Kim: any risks or blockers from Redwood side?
[09:06] Diego Alvarez: the main unknown is exact model perf at your token profiles — the perf run will clarify GPU count recommendation. Also if you require on-prem or strict private control plane, lead time grows.
[09:18] Nina Patel: timeline: procurement wants proposal by 2025-06-12 to make the quarterly budget. Can you hit that?
[09:24] Maya Chen: yes, we'll aim to deliver pricing + benchmark results within that window; action items noted.
[09:30] Diego Alvarez: we'll also include alternatives: smaller reserved baseline with burst credits vs larger reserved pool for guaranteed latency.
[09:39] Nina Patel: ok thanks, appreciate it.
[09:41] Maya Chen: thanks everyone. We'll follow up with docs and calendar invite for benchmark.

End transcript.
